data.body: Bug Bcc91b2328b. auto_id includes time_ns deliberately (two reports of the same text stay two records); ids.py docstring says 'stable for identical content' and knowledge.py bug_found says the same summary and item give the same auto id: both false. data.title: Auto ids are time-salted on purpose: correct the false determinism claims and pin the contract (fixes bug Bcc91b2328b)

chunk_findings.detail: The new sentence reads: "An id ddflow generates (no `--id`) is time-salted, so the same text filed twice gets two different ids; only the duplicate check, never the id, links a re-filing, and exact copies link automatically." The `on_match` policy is enumerated two sentences earlier in the same paragraph: `warn` "never refuses or merges — it lists the candidates and records the add as `new`" and `off` "skips the check entirely", and the following sentence confirms the check is what reads the log. So "exact copies link automatically" is false for two of the three supported settings: with `[dedupe].on_match = "off"`, `api.dedupe_check_add` is never invoked, so filing the same text twice produces two records with no link at all; with `on_match = "warn"`, the check runs but explicitly "never ... merges" and records the add as `new`, again with no automatic link. Only the default `ask` path auto-links. The same unconditional claim is repeated in `ddflow/core/ids.py` ("Two real reports of identical text stay two records until the add-time duplicate check ... exact copies are linked automatically"), whose "until ... links them" never fires under `off`/`warn`. The new text should gate the auto-link statement on the default policy, or state that `off`/`warn` leave identical re-filings as separate, unlinked records — which is exactly the "two records, no link" outcome the paragraph promises for those settings.

chunk_findings.detail: The test calls `auto_id("B", TEXT, "T1")` 50 times in a tight loop and asserts `len(ids) == 50`. Per the intent, the id's only source of variation is `time_ns` (the id is `B` + 10 hex chars, i.e. ~40 bits derived from kind/text/time). That makes this assertion a function of the platform clock granularity, not of the contract. On a platform where the system clock used by `time.time_ns()` has coarse resolution — most notably Windows, where `time.time_ns()` reports `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime` and updates only every ~15.6 ms — all 50 calls land in the same tick, produce the same `(kind, text, time_ns)` hash input, and therefore the same id. The set then has 1 element and `assert len(ids) == 50` fails, even though the source under test is correct. The same clock tick also breaks the very contract the test claims to pin ("two auto_id calls differ"); the test should therefore not assert 50 distinct ids unconditionally, since the guarantee only holds on fine-grained clocks. Demonstrate by running this file on Windows (or any environment with a millisecond-granularity wall clock): the loop completes in well under one tick and the assertion fails.

chunk_findings.detail:
The guard is a bare substring `re.search` over the whole source file, so it also rejects the *corrected* sentence that the fix is supposed to introduce. Concretely, the most natural rewrite of the ids.py claim is a negation, e.g.

    Auto ids are not stable for identical content; they include the time, so two calls differ.

With that input, `re.search(r"stable for identical content", text, re.I)` still matches the substring `stable for identical content` inside `not stable for identical content`, so the parametrized case fails with an AssertionError even though the false determinism claim has been removed. The same over-broad behavior applies to `r"content-addressed instead"` for a rewrite such as `...is not content-addressed instead...`. Because the assertion has no anchoring on the assertion form (it does not require the phrase to be absent of a preceding negation, nor does it match a full sentence), the test can fail on exactly the change it is meant to validate.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own intent states that the false determinism claim lives in two places — the `ids.py` docstring ("stable for identical content") and `knowledge.py`'s `bug_found` ("the same summary and item give the same auto id") — and that both are false ("Fix the comments"). The diff only rewrites the `ids.py` docstring and the README paragraph; `knowledge.py` is not in the diff at all. So after this change the `bug_found` documentation still promises callers a deterministic id: an agent that reads it and re-files an identical summary+item expecting the same auto id (e.g. to idempotently avoid a duplicate) instead gets a different time-salted id, and the only thing that saves it is the add-time duplicate check — exactly the behaviour the change set out to document correctly. The stale claim is the same defect being fixed in `ids.py`, just left behind; a caller who reads `bug_found`'s contract is still misled. Either the `knowledge.py` comment was supposed to be part of this fix (then it is missing), or the intent overstates what was fixed (then the wrong file was edited).
